migrationNotes: Spine: one garden tank, first with a steady tap, then a changing inflow, a starting amount and a leak, and finally the same sums on a car that goes forwards and then back, so the amount is always the start plus the integral of the net rate.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): cal-from-rate-to-amount-10 (3 L/min for 5 minutes), covered by the opening screens.
Prompts rewritten to stand alone: -2 (no longer says net rate before it is taught) and -7 (was the opener's question).

lesson.title: How much has changed?

lead.text: Take the steady tap first. Suppose the tank holds 10 litres when you start the clock, and the tap runs at 4 litres per minute for 6 minutes. Each minute adds 4 litres, so six minutes add 4 × 6 = 24 litres. That 24 litres is how much the amount changed. It is the change, and the tank holds more than that.
To find the amount, put the starting 10 litres back: 10 + 24 = 34 litres. The rate only told us what the tap added. What the tank holds is the starting amount plus that change.

afterFigure.text: The units confirm which quantity you have. A rate in litres per minute multiplied by a time in minutes leaves litres, so the result is an amount of water. On the graph of the rate, that amount is the area of the rectangle under it.

lead.text: Find the change first, then place it on top of what the tank held at the start.

reveal.text: The tap added 20 litres to the 30 already there, so the tank holds 50 litres. The 20 on its own is only the change.

lead.text: A real tap is seldom steady. Suppose it is eased open so that t minutes after you start, the inflow is 2t + 1 litres per minute. It begins at 1 litre per minute and grows steadily, so the graph of the rate is a sloping line and the area under it is no longer a rectangle.

The last lesson gave a method that works for any rate you can undo. Find an antiderivative F of the inflow. Put in the end time and the start time, then subtract. For 2t + 1 the antiderivative is F(t) = t² + t, so over the first 3 minutes F(3) − F(0) = 12 − 0 = 12 litres.

afterFigure.text: The graph agrees. The region under the line is a trapezoid 3 minutes wide, with heights 1 and 7 at its sides. The average of those heights is 4, so 4 × 3 = 12 litres. The result is in litres, so it is the change in the amount over the three minutes.

lead.text: Here is the same method written out on a different inflow.

steps.headline: Inflow is 4t + 1 litres per minute. How many litres enter from t = 0 to t = 3?

workedSteps.text: Put in the top end and the bottom end.

lead.text: Same plan: undo the rate, put in both ends and subtract.

reveal.text: You integrated the inflow over the interval and the result came out in litres, so it is the change in the tank.

lead.text: The integral gives the change over a stretch of time, and it makes no difference to the change what the tank held at the start. A tank that began with 5 litres and one that began with 500 gain exactly the same water from the same tap.
So the amount at time T is the amount at the start plus the integral of the rate from the start to T.

Take a tank holding 8 litres with an inflow of 4t litres per minute. Over the first 3 minutes the change is the integral of 4t, which has the antiderivative 2t². That gives 2 × 9 − 0 = 18 litres. The tank then holds 8 + 18 = 26 litres. This is the sum from the steady tap, with the 4 × 6 replaced by an integral.

steps.headline: A tank starts with 7 L and water flows in at 2t + 3 L/min. How much is in it at t = 2?

workedSteps.text: The change is the integral of the inflow.

lead.text: Now give the tank a leak. Water arrives at one rate and leaves at another, and what the tank does depends on the difference. With 9 litres per minute coming in and 4 going out, the tank gains 9 − 4 = 5 litres every minute. That difference is the net rate: the inflow minus the outflow.

The net rate is the rate at which the amount changes, so everything above applies to it. Integrate the net rate to get the change, then add the starting amount. Take an inflow of 2t litres per minute and a steady outflow of 3. The net rate is 2t − 3, an antiderivative is t² − 3t, and over the first 2 minutes the change is (4 − 6) − 0 = −2 litres.

afterFigure.text: The graph shows why the answer is negative. The net rate lies below the axis until t = 1.5, so the tank loses water at first and only refills after that. The signed area from the earlier lesson adds the two stretches: a loss of 2.25 litres and a gain of 0.25, which leaves −2 litres.

lead.text: Combine the two flows into a single rate.

reveal.text: Water leaving reduces the gain, so you subtract the outflow from the inflow to get the net rate.

steps.headline: The same sum for a moving car

lead.text: Nothing in the method belongs to water. A car's velocity is the rate at which its position changes, so the same steps apply. Integrate the velocity over a stretch of time and you get the displacement, which is the change in position. Add the position the car started from and you have where it is now.

Velocity has a sign. It is positive going forwards and negative going backwards, so forward travel and backward travel cancel in the integral. Take v(t) = 4 − 2t metres per second for 3 seconds. The car moves forward until t = 2, where the velocity reaches zero. After that it reverses. An antiderivative is 4t − t², so the displacement is (12 − 9) − 0 = 3 metres.

afterFigure.text: The distance driven is a different quantity, because it counts all the ground covered whichever way the car faces. Going forwards the car covers ½ × 2 × 4 = 4 metres. Going back it covers ½ × 1 × 2 = 1 metre. The distance is 4 + 1 = 5 metres, while the displacement is 4 − 1 = 3 metres. Distance is the integral of speed, which is the size of the velocity with the sign removed.

lead.text: Split the trip where the velocity changes sign, and compare what the signs do to each total.

reveal.text: The forward and backward stretches are equal in length. Displacement keeps their signs and cancels, and distance adds their sizes.

lead.text: Back to the tank, now with an inflow that changes and a steady leak. Find the net change over the first two minutes.

reveal.text: You subtracted the rates first and then integrated the net rate. The change in the amount is the integral of the net rate.

lesson.orientation: Recover amounts from net rates while keeping track of starting values and direction.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A water tank in a garden has a gauge you cannot read, because the glass has clouded over. What you do have is the dial on the tap, which says how many litres per minute are running in, and a note you wrote last week of how much the tank held then. From those two pieces of information you want to know how much is in the tank now.

This is the last lesson put to work. A rate, added up over a stretch of time, gives the change in an amount. It does not give the amount itself, and that matters as soon as the tank did not start empty. A tank with a leak adds a further need, which is a way to handle water going out as well as coming in.

We start with a steady tap and then let it change. After that we add the leak. At the end the same arithmetic describes a car that drives forwards and then back, which shows that nothing in the method belongs to water.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn a rate into the change it causes, and add the starting amount to find what is there.
intro.whyItMatters: Water, money and distance are all amounts built from rates.

recap.keyIdea: Integrating a rate over an interval gives the change in the amount. Add the starting amount to get the amount itself.

blocks.text: A tank that began with 30 litres and gained 5 litres a minute held 50 litres after 4 minutes. An inflow of 2t + 3 gave 10 litres in two minutes, and 17 litres in the tank once its starting 7 were added. A net rate of 3t + 2 gave a change of 10 litres too, and a car with velocity 3t − 2 from a start of 5 metres reached 7 metres.

recap.nextHook: That closes the course. You can now go from an amount to its rate by differentiating and from a rate back to an amount by integrating, and the fundamental theorem is what joins the two.

questions.prompt: Water enters at r(t) = 2t + 3 litres per minute. How many litres enter from t = 0 to t = 2 minutes?
hints: Accumulate the rate over the whole interval.
An antiderivative of the inflow is a quadratic plus a linear term.
Evaluate its endpoint difference over the requested time interval.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Integrate the rate: [t² + 3t] from 0 to 2 gives 4 + 6 = 10 L.

questions.onCorrect: 10 L. Integrate the rate over the interval: 4 + 6.

misconceptions.feedback: 7 is the rate at t = 2. The question asks for the amount over the interval.
Integrate each term: the 3 contributes too.

questions.prompt: A tank starts with 7 L. Water flows in at 2t + 3 L/min for 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. How many litres are present at t = 2?
hints: The integral gives the change, which must be added to the starting amount.
First evaluate the integral of the net inflow over the interval.
Add this change to the starting volume.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The net change is 10 L, so the final amount is 7 + 10 = 17 L.

questions.onCorrect: 17 L. The change, 10 L, added to the starting 7 L.

misconceptions.feedback: 10 L is the change. Add the starting amount.
7 L is only the starting amount. Add the change.

questions.prompt: For velocity v(t) = 2t − 2 m/s on [0, 2], which statement is true?
hints: Use velocity for signed change and its magnitude for distance.

acceptedIdeas: Displacement is zero and distance is two metres
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The negative and positive triangular displacements cancel; their magnitudes add to 2 m.

choices.label: Displacement is zero and distance is two metres
Both displacement and distance are zero

questions.onCorrect: Displacement is zero and distance is 2 m: signed velocity cancels, speed does not.

misconceptions.feedback: The forward and backward parts both have length. Distance adds their sizes.
Displacement keeps signs, so the backward part subtracts.

questions.prompt: Inflow is 3t + 4 L/min and outflow is 2 L/min. Find the net change in litres from t = 0 to t = 2.
hints: Subtract the rates before integrating.
The net rate equals inflow minus outflow at each time.
Integrate the net linear rate and evaluate its endpoint difference.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Net rate is 3t + 2. Its integral is [1.5t² + 2t] from 0 to 2 = 10 L.

questions.onCorrect: 10 L. Net rate 3t + 2, integrated over the interval.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the inflow alone. Subtract the outflow as well.

questions.prompt: Position starts at 5 m and velocity is v(t) = 3t − 2 m/s. Find position at t = 2 seconds in metres.
hints: Add signed displacement to initial position.
Integrate velocity to get signed displacement over the interval.
Add displacement to the initial position.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Displacement is [1.5t² − 2t] from 0 to 2 = 2 m. Add the initial 5 m to obtain 7 m.

questions.onCorrect: 7 m. A displacement of 2 m added to the starting 5 m.

misconceptions.feedback: 2 m is the displacement. Add the starting position.
5 m is only the starting position. Add the displacement.

questions.prompt: A rate has units litres per minute and is integrated with respect to minutes. What are the resulting units?
hints: Multiply the rate units by the integration variable's units.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The time unit cancels, leaving an accumulated volume in litres.

choices.label: A change in flow rate, measured in L/min²
A reciprocal flow rate, measured in min/L

questions.onCorrect: Litres. The minutes cancel, leaving an accumulated volume.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be differentiating the rate. Integrating multiplies by time.
Integrating does not invert the rate. It multiplies it by time.

questions.prompt: A tank holds 30 litres. Water flows in at a steady 5 litres per minute for 4 minutes. How many litres are in the tank after those 4 minutes?
hints: How much water is added in 4 minutes?
20 L is added. Was the tank empty at the start?
Add the starting 30 L.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It gains 5 × 4 = 20 L, on top of the 30 L it began with: 50 L.

questions.onCorrect: 50. The amount is the starting amount plus the change.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the water added. The tank started with some.
That is the starting amount. Add the water that came in.

questions.prompt: Why does the answer come out in litres?
hints: What happens to the minutes when you multiply by a time?

acceptedIdeas: Litres per minute times minutes leaves litres
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The rate is in litres per minute and the width is in minutes, so the minutes cancel.

choices.label: Litres per minute times minutes leaves litres

questions.onCorrect: Litres per minute times minutes leaves litres.

misconceptions.feedback: The units come from the arithmetic: look at what multiplying by minutes does to L/min.
The units depend on the rate. This rate is in litres per minute.

questions.prompt: A tank holds 40 L. Inflow is 2t L/min and outflow is 6 L/min for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4. How many litres are in the tank at t = 4?
hints: First find the net rate: inflow minus outflow.
The net rate is 2t − 6. Integrate it from 0 to 4.
The change is negative. Add it to the starting 40 L.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The net rate is 2t − 6. Its integral is t² − 6t, which is 16 − 24 = −8 over 0 to 4. The tank holds 40 − 8 = 32 L.

questions.onCorrect: 32. Net rate, integrate for the change, then add the starting amount.

misconceptions.feedback: −8 L is the change. Add it to the starting amount.
That is only the starting amount. Add the net change.

questions.prompt: A rate of 3 L/min runs for 5 minutes. What change does it give, in litres?
hints: What do you multiply a rate by to get an amount?
Multiply by the time.
What is 3 × 5?
questions.onCorrect: 15. A steady rate times its time is the change.

misconceptions.feedback: Rates multiply by time. They are not added to it.

questions.prompt: Inflow is 7 L/min and outflow is 4 L/min. What is the net rate, in L/min?
hints: Is the water leaving a gain or a loss?
Take the loss off the gain.
questions.onCorrect: 3. Water leaving reduces the rate of gain.

misconceptions.feedback: Outflow takes water away, so subtract it.
